title: ParaRecover: A Process-Level Benchmark for Error Localization and Recovery in Parallel Tool-Use Agents

    Title:ParaRecover: A Process-Level Benchmark for Error Localization and Recovery in Parallel Tool-Use Agents

            Abstract:Existing agent benchmarks mainly evaluate final task success or tool-call correctness, providing limited insight into whether agents can reliably diagnose and recover from intermediate execution failures. This limitation becomes particularly critical in multi-turn parallel tool-use scenarios, where errors may propagate across dependent branches and trigger cascading failures. We introduce ParaRecover, a process-level benchmark for evaluating error localization and recovery in multi-turn parallel tool-use agents. Built upon a fine-grained taxonomy of 14 error types covering planning dependencies, tool selection, and argument matching, the benchmark comprises 10,626 instances spanning two difficulty levels. To enable finegrained, process-oriented evaluation, we further propose the SDE rubric, which measures structural integrity, diagnostic reasoning, and evolutionary strategy during agent this http URL across more than ten mainstream LLMs reveal that even state-of-the-art models still struggle with multi-turn error propagation,implicit tool-use failures, and precise replanning. Moreover, we demonstrate that the SDE rubric provides effective supervision signals for improving agents' reflective recovery capabilities. Our data and code are available at this https URL.

report.summary: ParaRecover is a process-level benchmark testing whether parallel tool-use AI agents can localize and recover from intermediate execution errors, not just complete tasks.
report.background: Most agent benchmarks score only final task success or whether individual tool calls were syntactically correct. That works when an agent runs a single linear chain, but modern assistants increasingly fan out across parallel tool calls, sub-agents and dependent branches. In those settings a small mistake in one branch can silently corrupt downstream steps, producing cascading failures that a pass/fail score never exposes. Developers therefore lack a way to tell whether a model truly understands why something broke, or simply got lucky on a retry. ParaRecover, submitted to arXiv in September 2026, targets this gap by shifting evaluation from outcomes to process: it asks whether an agent can identify where a failure occurred, explain it, and replan. The work lands as labs race to ship long-horizon agents for coding, research and enterprise workflows, where reliability under partial failure is the main blocker to deployment.
key_points: The benchmark is built on a fine-grained taxonomy of 14 error types, covering planning dependencies, tool selection and argument matching. It contains 10,626 instances split across two difficulty levels, letting researchers measure specific failure modes rather than a single aggregate score.

Instead of grading only the final answer, ParaRecover scores the agent's trajectory with a new SDE rubric: structural integrity of the execution graph, diagnostic reasoning about what went wrong, and the evolutionary strategy used to replan and recover.

Tests across more than ten mainstream LLMs show that even state-of-the-art models struggle with multi-turn error propagation, implicit tool-use failures that never throw an explicit error, and precise replanning after a fault.

The authors show the SDE rubric doubles as a supervision signal: using it to train or guide agents measurably improves their reflective recovery ability, suggesting process-level scoring can be a training objective, not just a report card.

Parallel tool use is the sharpest edge case. Because branches depend on each other, an unnoticed error in one call can trigger cascading failures across the whole execution tree, which outcome-only benchmarks systematically hide.
report.impact: For the AI industry, ParaRecover pushes agent evaluation from 'did it work?' toward 'can it be trusted when it breaks?' — a shift that matters for any vendor selling long-running autonomous agents. For developers, it supplies a shared taxonomy and metric to debug orchestration layers, compare models on recovery rather than raw capability, and generate supervision data for fine-tuning. For regular users, the practical payoff is agents that notice their own mistakes, explain them and try a different route instead of confidently returning corrupted results — the difference between a demo and a dependable assistant for bookings, code changes or financial tasks. Expect reliability, not raw benchmark scores, to become the main competitive axis.
report.tools: The paper's dataset and code are released alongside it on arXiv, so start there. For context, compare against agent benchmarks like AgentBench, τ-bench and ToolBench, and SWE-bench for coding agents. To instrument your own agents with process-level tracing, look at LangSmith, LangFuse, AgentOps and OpenTelemetry-based tracing, plus orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, AutoGen and the OpenAI Agents SDK, which expose the branch structure ParaRecover evaluates.
